questions.question: A Linux administrator needs to load the kernel module `e1000e` into the running kernel so a newly-installed NIC is recognised without rebooting. Which command loads the module and any modules it depends on?
options: `modinfo e1000e` — prints metadata (author, parameters, dependencies) without loading the module
`modprobe e1000e` — resolves the module's dependency chain in modules.dep and inserts them in order
`insmod e1000e` — expects a full path to a `.ko` file and does not resolve dependencies
`lsmod e1000e` — reads /proc/modules to list loaded modules and ignores extra arguments
questions.explanation: `modprobe e1000e` reads /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/modules.dep, walks the module's dependency chain and inserts each `.ko` in the right order, so it is the standard way to add a driver to a running kernel. `insmod` inserts a single module from an absolute path and does NOT resolve dependencies, so if e1000e needs mii or ptp preloaded it will simply fail. `modinfo` prints module metadata (author, license, parameters) and never modifies kernel state. `lsmod` reads /proc/modules to list the modules that are already loaded — it takes no filename argument and cannot load anything.

questions.question: After an unclean shutdown a RHEL box drops to `emergency.target` with `Failed to mount /data` on an ext4 partition. Which command should the administrator run FIRST from the emergency shell to check and repair the unmounted /data filesystem?
options: `mount -o remount,rw /data` — asks the kernel to remount an ext4 volume that has not yet passed a consistency check
`fsck -y /dev/sdb1` — runs fsck auto-answering yes to every prompt, including risky repairs on complex corruption
`xfs_repair /dev/sdb1` — only understands XFS metadata and refuses to touch an ext2/3/4 superblock
`e2fsck -f /dev/sdb1` — forces a full ext-family check even if the superblock is flagged clean
questions.explanation: `e2fsck -f` is the ext-family repair tool: `-f` forces a full check even when the superblock's clean bit is set, which is exactly what you want after an unclean shutdown that may have left the journal in a suspect state. `fsck -y /dev/sdb1` dispatches to e2fsck for ext4 but the `-y` flag answers yes to every prompt including risky reallocations — safer to run e2fsck interactively. `mount -o remount,rw /data` cannot remount a filesystem that is not currently mounted (and would just re-hit the same error). `xfs_repair` only knows XFS on-disk format and refuses to run against an ext4 superblock.

questions.question: A sysadmin has written a new systemd service unit `appd.service` and wants `systemctl enable appd` to start the service automatically when the system reaches `multi-user.target`. Which directive belongs in the [Install] section of the unit?
options: `WantedBy=multi-user.target` — enable creates a symlink in multi-user.target.wants/ so the target pulls it in
`After=multi-user.target` — only orders start-up, no autostart symlink is created
`Requires=multi-user.target` — declares a dependency but does not register the unit with a target
`RequiredBy=multi-user.target` — not a valid [Install] directive on any released systemd version
questions.explanation: `WantedBy=multi-user.target` in the [Install] section is what `systemctl enable` looks for: it creates the symlink `/etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/appd.service`, so when systemd reaches multi-user.target the unit is pulled in and started. `After=` belongs in [Unit] and only orders start-up relative to another unit — it never causes autostart. `Requires=` also belongs in [Unit]; it declares a hard dependency but again does not register the unit with a target for enablement. `RequiredBy=` is not a recognised directive on shipping systemd releases (only `WantedBy=` and `RequiredBy=` documentation confusion — the actual [Install] keys are `WantedBy`, `Also`, `Alias`, `DefaultInstance`).

questions.question: An administrator needs to create a new 10 GiB logical volume called `datalv` inside an existing LVM2 volume group `datavg`. Which command creates it?
options: `vgcreate -L 10G datalv datavg` — creates a volume GROUP, not an LV, and takes PV devices as arguments
`lvcreate -s 10G -n datalv datavg` — the `-s` flag creates a snapshot of an existing LV, not a fresh volume
`lvcreate -L 10G -n datalv datavg` — `-L` sets the size, `-n` sets the name, VG name comes last
`pvcreate -L 10G -n datalv datavg` — pvcreate initialises a physical volume and accepts neither `-L` nor `-n`
questions.explanation: `lvcreate -L 10G -n datalv datavg` is the canonical form: `-L` sets an absolute size (use `-l` for extent counts or percentages), `-n` names the new LV, and the positional argument is the target volume group. `lvcreate -s` in that form is a snapshot request — it needs the origin LV, not a VG. `vgcreate` builds a volume GROUP from initialised PVs; it does not create logical volumes at all. `pvcreate` initialises a block device as a physical volume and rejects the `-L`/`-n` flags shown here.

questions.question: A security policy requires that the account `jsmith` be prevented from logging in with a password RIGHT NOW, without deleting the account, its home directory or its data. Which command achieves that?
options: `chage -I -1 jsmith` — sets password inactivity to -1 which disables the inactivity feature, it does not lock the account
`usermod -L jsmith` — prefixes the /etc/shadow password hash with `!`, so no password can match
`passwd -e jsmith` — expires the password so the user MUST change it on next login, but they can still log in
`userdel -r jsmith` — deletes the user AND their home directory, which the policy explicitly forbids
questions.explanation: `usermod -L jsmith` (equivalent to `passwd -l`) locks the account by prepending `!` to the hash in /etc/shadow, so no supplied password can ever match — the account and its data are untouched. `passwd -e` only marks the password as expired: the user is forced to set a new one on next login but is not actually blocked. `chage -I -1` explicitly disables the inactivity feature, which is the opposite of locking. `userdel -r` removes the user entry AND the home directory, which violates the requirement to keep the data intact.

questions.question: On a UEFI-booted system running GRUB2, the administrator wants to change the boot-menu timeout so the user has more time to pick an older kernel entry. Which file should they edit and then regenerate grub.cfg from?
options: `/boot/grub2/grub.cfg` — the compiled menu; editing it directly is overwritten on the next grub2-mkconfig
`/etc/grub.d/40_custom` — for adding CUSTOM menu entries, not for changing global settings like the timeout
`/boot/grub2/grubenv` — a key/value environment file that stores `saved_entry`, not the timeout
`/etc/default/grub` — holds `GRUB_TIMEOUT=` and friends, consumed by grub2-mkconfig when it rebuilds grub.cfg
questions.explanation: `/etc/default/grub` is where you set `GRUB_TIMEOUT=`, `GRUB_DEFAULT=`, `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX=` and similar knobs; `grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg` then bakes them into the actual menu. `/boot/grub2/grub.cfg` IS the compiled menu and is stamped as auto-generated — hand edits are wiped on the next `grub2-mkconfig` run. `/etc/grub.d/40_custom` is the drop-in for hand-authored menu entries (rescue images, extra distros); it does not hold the timeout. `/boot/grub2/grubenv` is a small block-aligned env file that stores runtime state such as `saved_entry`, not menu configuration.

questions.question: `chage -l alice` prints `Password expires: Mar 01, 2026`. It is now late April 2026 and Alice can still log in with her password. What is the MOST likely reason her expired password is still accepted?
options: The `INACTIVE` field in /etc/shadow grants a grace period after expiry during which the password still works (with a forced change)
PAM has been reconfigured to ignore /etc/shadow expiry — the default `pam_unix` configuration would normally block her
`chage` reads a different source than /etc/shadow, so the tool's report is out of date compared to the real hash file
SSH public-key authentication bypasses password expiry — even though the scenario says she is entering a password
questions.explanation: The `INACTIVE` field (column 7 in /etc/shadow) sets how many days AFTER the password expiry the account still accepts logins, forcing a password change on entry. Set it to a large value and the user keeps working past the printed expiry date. `pam_unix` on a default system honours shadow expiry, so "PAM ignores expiry" is not the default explanation. `chage` reads /etc/shadow directly, so its report cannot be stale compared to shadow. SSH public-key auth would bypass expiry, but the scenario explicitly says Alice logs in with her password, so keys are not what is happening.

questions.question: A batch process with PID 1234 is currently running and needs to be given the lowest possible CPU scheduling priority (nice value +19) WITHOUT stopping or pausing it. Which command is correct?
options: `nice -n 19 1234` — `nice` only applies to a command being started, it cannot re-nice an existing PID
`renice +19 1234` — the classic (non-POSIX) short form; deprecated on many distros in favour of `renice -n`
`renice -n 19 -p 1234` — POSIX form: `-n 19` sets the new nice value, `-p 1234` targets the running PID
`nice --adjustment=19 -p 1234` — `nice` has no `-p` option and `--adjustment` is not a recognised long form
questions.explanation: `renice -n 19 -p 1234` is the POSIX-portable syntax to re-nice an existing process: `-n` sets the new nice value (+19 is the lowest priority) and `-p` selects the PID. `nice` launches a NEW command with a modified nice value; it cannot address an already-running PID. `renice +19 1234` is the older BSD-style short form and still works on Linux, but it is not POSIX and some distros prefer the `-n` form for scripts. `nice --adjustment=19 -p 1234` is invalid — `nice` accepts `-n` (or `--adjustment`) only as a modifier to a command it is about to spawn, and it has no `-p` option.

questions.question: After a package upgrade the administrator wants to check whether any installed file from the `httpd` RPM has been modified since installation (size, checksum, mode). Which command performs that verification against the RPM database?
options: `rpm -qi httpd` — prints package metadata (version, summary, description); does not check file integrity
`rpm --checksig httpd.rpm` — checks the GPG signature of a .rpm file on disk, not the installed files
`rpm -V httpd` — verifies each installed file against the RPM database (mode, size, MD5/SHA, mtime, owner)
`rpm -Vf httpd` — takes a FILE path, not a package name, so `httpd` as a bare name is not valid input
questions.explanation: `rpm -V httpd` (verify) walks every file the package installed and compares it against the RPM database: size, hash, mode, owner, group, mtime, capabilities. Discrepancies are shown as a code column (`S.5....T.` etc.). `rpm -qi` prints metadata and never touches the files themselves. `rpm --checksig` validates the GPG signature of a `.rpm` file — useful before installation, but says nothing about files already on disk. `rpm -Vf` expects a filesystem PATH to identify which package to verify (`rpm -Vf /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf`); passing a package name to `-Vf` is not the correct usage.

questions.question: On a legacy Debian server, `apt update` fails because a repository's signing key is missing (short key ID `ABCD1234`). The administrator wants to import that key from `keyserver.ubuntu.com` into the APT trusted keyring. Which command does the job?
options: `apt-key add ABCD1234` — `apt-key add` reads a key from a FILE or stdin; it does not know how to fetch from a keyserver
`apt-key adv --keyserver hkp://keyserver.ubuntu.com --recv-keys ABCD1234` — invokes gpg to fetch the key and adds it to /etc/apt/trusted.gpg
`dpkg --add-key ABCD1234` — `dpkg` has no `--add-key` sub-command; this is invented syntax
`gpg --recv-keys ABCD1234` — fetches the key into the USER's GnuPG keyring, not the APT trusted keyring
questions.explanation: `apt-key adv --keyserver hkp://keyserver.ubuntu.com --recv-keys ABCD1234` is the traditional recipe: `adv` passes the remaining flags straight to `gpg` on the trusted APT keyring, so the key is fetched from the given keyserver and added to /etc/apt/trusted.gpg (or /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d). `apt-key add` only reads bytes from stdin or a supplied file — there is no keyserver mode. `dpkg --add-key` does not exist. `gpg --recv-keys` succeeds but drops the key into the invoking USER's keyring, which APT does not consult, so `apt update` still fails. (Modern releases prefer signed-by= and /etc/apt/keyrings/, but for classic `apt-key`-based systems this is the answer.)

questions.question: A systemd unit with `Type=forking` fails to start; the journal shows `Timeout waiting for PID file`. What is the MOST likely misconfiguration in the unit file?
options: The unit's `PIDFile=` directive is missing or points to a path the daemon never writes
`Type=simple` should be used instead — forking mode is deprecated in current systemd releases
The `ExecStart=` binary is missing from disk, which produces this timeout instead of an execve error
`[Install] WantedBy=` is not set, and systemd refuses to start units that are not enabled to a target
questions.explanation: When `Type=forking` is set, systemd starts the initial process, expects it to fork, expects the parent to exit, and then waits for the daemon's PID file to appear so it can track the surviving child. A missing or mistyped `PIDFile=` produces exactly the observed `Timeout waiting for PID file` error. `Type=simple` (not forking) is the systemd-preferred style but is not deprecated — traditional daemons that fork legitimately still need `forking`. A missing ExecStart binary raises `status=203/EXEC` immediately, not a PID-file timeout. `[Install] WantedBy=` only affects whether `systemctl enable` creates a symlink; it does not gate manual starts.

questions.question: After running `lvextend -L +20G /dev/datavg/datalv`, the underlying XFS filesystem mounted at `/data` still reports the old size. Which command grows the XFS filesystem to fill the new LV?
options: `fsck.xfs /data` — a no-op on Linux (returns 0 immediately); XFS does not have an offline fsck of this shape
`resize2fs /dev/datavg/datalv` — the ext2/3/4 resizer, refuses to touch an XFS superblock
`xfs_growfs /data` — grows the mounted XFS filesystem to its underlying block device size
`xfs_repair -n /dev/datavg/datalv` — dry-run repair, does not grow anything and needs the FS unmounted
questions.explanation: `xfs_growfs` extends a MOUNTED XFS filesystem to the current size of its block device, which is exactly what you need after the underlying LV was extended. XFS was designed to only grow online — there is no offline grow tool. `resize2fs` is the ext-family resizer and refuses to operate on the XFS on-disk format. `xfs_repair -n` runs a read-only check (dry run) and additionally requires the filesystem to be unmounted, so it can neither grow the FS nor be run against `/data` while mounted. `fsck.xfs` is a stub that returns success — real XFS integrity work is done by `xfs_repair`, not `fsck.xfs`.

questions.question: The administrator wants `/backup` (ext4) to auto-mount at boot, keyed by UUID (so it survives sdX renaming), READ-ONLY, and included in normal fsck passes. Which /etc/fstab line meets ALL of those requirements?
options: `/dev/sdc1  /backup  ext4  ro,defaults  0  2` — uses the device name (defeats UUID stability); `defaults` also implies `rw`
`UUID=abc123  /backup  ext4  ro  0  2` — UUID-keyed, mounted read-only, fsck pass 2 (non-root)
`UUID=abc123  /backup  ext4  defaults  0  0` — `defaults` includes `rw` and pass 0 skips fsck entirely
`UUID=abc123  /backup  ext4  ro,noatime  0  0` — read-only is correct, but pass 0 disables the fsck pass
questions.explanation: `UUID=abc123 /backup ext4 ro 0 2` ticks every requirement: UUID stops the entry from breaking when /dev/sdc becomes /dev/sdd, `ro` mounts read-only, dump field 0 skips dump(8) (deprecated), and pass 2 tells `fsck` to check non-root filesystems in parallel after the root. The other three fail at least one requirement: option A hard-codes the /dev name AND uses `defaults` (implies rw); option C uses `defaults` (implies rw) and disables fsck by using pass 0; option D correctly mounts read-only but uses pass 0, which explicitly opts the partition out of boot-time fsck.

questions.question: After `useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G wheel devuser`, /etc/passwd shows devuser's PRIMARY group as `devuser`, not `wheel`. Why?
options: The wheel group is missing on this box, so useradd silently fell back to a default private group
`-G` sets the primary group, so useradd overrode it with the passwd defaults from /etc/login.defs
`-m` implies primary-group creation and takes precedence over any group flag on the same command line
`useradd` creates a user-private primary group named after the user by default; `-G wheel` only adds wheel as a SUPPLEMENTARY group
questions.explanation: By default (`USERGROUPS_ENAB yes` in /etc/login.defs), `useradd` creates a private group named after the user and makes it the primary group. `-G` is exclusively for SUPPLEMENTARY groups; the primary is set with lowercase `-g`. If `wheel` did NOT exist, useradd would fail with an error rather than fall back silently — so option A is wrong. `-m` controls whether the home directory is created and copied from /etc/skel; it does not touch group assignment. So `devuser` is the primary group, and `wheel` is a supplementary group as requested.

questions.question: A developer's script at `/opt/readcert.sh` (owned by root) must read files in `/etc/ssl/private` (root-owned) WITHOUT giving the developer full root access. Which configuration best satisfies least-privilege?
options: Dedicated group `sslreaders`: add the developer to it, chgrp the key directory to it, set mode 750 on the directory (640 on files inside)
`chmod 4755 /opt/readcert.sh` — set SUID so the script always runs as root; Linux, however, ignores SUID on interpreted scripts as a well-known race-condition mitigation
Add the developer to the `root` group and set `/etc/ssl/private` to 640 — but the root group grants access to root-group-owned files scattered across the entire system, not just SSL keys
`chmod +t /etc/ssl/private` — set the sticky bit on the directory; sticky only prevents non-owners from DELETING files inside, it has no effect at all on read permission
questions.explanation: Least privilege is a dedicated group: create `sslreaders`, add just the developer, change group ownership on `/etc/ssl/private` (and the key files inside it), then `chmod 750` on the directory and `640` on the files. The developer gets exactly the reads they need and nothing else. Setting SUID on a shell script is a common trap — the Linux kernel deliberately ignores the SUID bit on interpreted scripts to close a well-known race window, so `chmod 4755` does nothing useful. Adding a user to the `root` group grants read access to every root-group-owned file on the box, far beyond `/etc/ssl/private`. The sticky bit on a directory only prevents users from deleting files they do not own; it has no effect on read permission.

questions.question: `ps aux` shows PID 4521 pinning a CPU at 98%. The administrator wants to give it a chance to shut down cleanly, then force-kill it only if it will not exit. In what order should the signals be sent?
options: SIGHUP (1), then SIGTERM (15), then SIGKILL (9) — SIGHUP is a config-reload/hangup signal, not a shutdown request
SIGKILL (9), then SIGTERM (15) — SIGKILL immediately terminates and cannot be caught, so nothing else runs afterwards
SIGTERM (15), then SIGKILL (9) — SIGTERM asks the process to clean up and exit; SIGKILL forces it if it refuses
SIGSTOP (19), then SIGTERM (15) — SIGSTOP pauses the process (T state) but does not shut it down at all
questions.explanation: The graceful-then-forceful pattern is SIGTERM → wait → SIGKILL. SIGTERM (15) is the default `kill` signal and asks the process to clean up (flush buffers, run atexit handlers, release locks) before exiting; SIGKILL (9) is the fallback that the kernel delivers unconditionally, so no cleanup runs. Starting with SIGKILL destroys any chance of cleanup. SIGHUP historically meant hangup and modern daemons repurpose it for config reload — it is not a shutdown request. SIGSTOP simply pauses the process into the T state; it neither asks it to exit nor terminates it.

questions.question: The `pcspkr` kernel module keeps loading and producing a system beep. The administrator wants to stop it from loading automatically at boot from now on. Which single action is the CORRECT persistent fix?
options: `echo 'blacklist pcspkr' > /etc/modprobe.d/nobeep.conf` — persists across reboots; modprobe skips blacklisted modules on autoload
`echo 'blacklist pcspkr' >> /etc/modules` — /etc/modules is a load-on-boot LIST, not a blacklist file
`rmmod pcspkr` — unloads the module RIGHT NOW but nothing prevents it from being autoloaded again on next boot
Set `install pcspkr /bin/true` on the command line — this is the runtime form; without a config file it does not persist
questions.explanation: Dropping `blacklist pcspkr` into a file under `/etc/modprobe.d/` (with a `.conf` suffix) is what modprobe reads at every boot and on hotplug events, so the module is never autoloaded again. `/etc/modules` (Debian) does the opposite — it lists modules to be LOADED at boot. `rmmod pcspkr` removes it from the running kernel but leaves nothing on disk, so the next boot loads it again. `install pcspkr /bin/true` is a stronger override that has to live in a modprobe.d file too; giving it on the command line does not persist, so this option describes the mechanism but not a durable configuration.

questions.question: GRUB2 dropped the system to the `grub rescue>` prompt. `ls` reports `(hd0) (hd0,gpt1) (hd0,gpt2)`, where /boot lives on `(hd0,gpt2)`. Which sequence of commands boots the running system to userspace?
options: `insmod normal` then `normal` — that only works from the FULL GRUB shell once modules load; from `grub rescue>` you need the rescue-mode sequence
`grub-install (hd0); update-grub; boot` — `grub-install` and `update-grub` require a booted OS and cannot run from the rescue prompt
`boot (hd0,gpt2)/vmlinuz root=/dev/sda2` — GRUB rescue has no `boot IMAGE` form; you must first set root, load linux and initrd, then run boot
`set prefix=(hd0,gpt2)/grub2; set root=(hd0,gpt2); insmod normal; normal` — sets prefix/root, loads the normal module, then hands off to the standard GRUB menu
questions.explanation: From `grub rescue>` the rescue shell only has a tiny built-in command set; the recovery pattern is to tell it where GRUB's modules live (`set prefix=(hd0,gpt2)/grub2`), set root, then load `insmod normal` and enter normal mode, which finds grub.cfg and boots as usual. Option A skips the required prefix/root setup and cannot find `normal.mod` on its own. Option B calls tools (`grub-install`, `update-grub`) that need a running Linux userspace — you are trying to get there. Option C uses a syntax `boot IMAGE` that GRUB2 does not accept; the correct hand-boot sequence is `linux ...; initrd ...; boot` — a single `boot IMAGE` line is not valid.

questions.question: A RHEL server's `journalctl -xe` shows `kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 3201 (java) score 890`. What has happened?
options: The Java Virtual Machine threw a `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError` and the JVM aborted itself — this shows up as a JVM stack trace, not a kernel message
The Linux kernel's OOM killer terminated the java process because the system ran out of memory; the score reflects how heavily OOM targets it
The process exceeded a per-process `ulimit -v` memory cap; ulimit denials surface as `Cannot allocate memory` from libc, not as kernel OOM messages
A cgroup memory limit was reached and cgroup-OOM stepped in; cgroup-OOM logs include `Memory cgroup out of memory:` not the plain kernel form
questions.explanation: The plain-kernel `Out of memory: Killed process ... score N` log line is the SYSTEM-wide OOM killer firing when free memory plus reclaimable is exhausted. The oom_score is a per-process ranking that the killer uses to pick a victim. A JVM heap-space error surfaces from Java (`java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`), not from the kernel journal. `ulimit -v` denials are reported by libc as EN0MEM/`Cannot allocate memory` on the calling syscall — they don't ride the OOM code path. cgroup memory limits produce a slightly different log prefix (`Memory cgroup out of memory:` / `Memory cgroup stats for /...`) that would appear alongside the container path, which the sample line does not include.

questions.question: After rebooting a system, an administrator notices that a custom service file at `/etc/systemd/system/myapp.service` was edited on disk but systemd still uses the OLD contents. Which command tells systemd to re-read unit files from disk without restarting the service?
options: `systemctl reset-failed myapp` — clears the FAILED state flag; does not re-read unit files
`systemctl reload myapp` — asks the SERVICE (via SIGHUP or ExecReload=) to reload its own config, not systemd itself
`systemctl daemon-reload` — re-parses every unit file from disk and rebuilds systemd's in-memory dependency graph
`systemctl restart myapp` — restarts the process using systemd's CACHED copy of the old unit file
questions.explanation: `systemctl daemon-reload` is the exact command for this scenario: it re-reads every unit file from disk (including your edited `myapp.service`), rebuilds the dependency graph and applies the new configuration to the systemd manager. `systemctl restart` alone uses the CACHED unit that daemon-reload has not yet refreshed, so the edits are ignored. `systemctl reload` sends the service its own `ExecReload=` (or SIGHUP) so the running daemon rereads ITS config file — not systemd's unit. `reset-failed` only clears the FAILED marker so the next start attempt is allowed; it does not refresh unit files.

questions.question: Which numeric-notation `chmod` sets `/opt/script.sh` to `rwxr-x---` (owner rwx, group r-x, other no access)?
options: `chmod 755 /opt/script.sh` — sets other=r-x (5), granting world execute which the requirement forbids
`chmod 750 /opt/script.sh` — owner=rwx (7), group=r-x (5), other=--- (0), matching the requirement exactly
`chmod 740 /opt/script.sh` — sets group=r-- (4), stripping execute from the group which the requirement requires
`chmod 754 /opt/script.sh` — sets other=r-- (4), granting world read which the requirement forbids
questions.explanation: Decoding `rwxr-x---`: owner rwx=4+2+1=7, group r-x=4+0+1=5, other ---=0, so the mode is `750`. `755` adds r-x for other, which the requirement forbids. `740` strips execute from the group (`r--` = 4). `754` grants read to other (`r--` = 4), also forbidden. Only `750` matches the exact rwx pattern given.

questions.question: A security audit reports that /etc/passwd is world-writable. What is the CORRECT permission mode to restore — readable by everyone (many utilities depend on it), writable only by root?
options: `chmod 444 /etc/passwd` — makes it read-only for root as well, breaking password/user changes system-wide
`chmod 600 /etc/passwd` — root-only read/write; strips read from ordinary users and breaks user-lookup calls
`chmod 644 /etc/passwd` — root rw, everyone read; matches the reference mode shipped by every major distro
`chmod 640 /etc/passwd` — removes read for `other`, so unprivileged tools cannot resolve UIDs to names
questions.explanation: The canonical mode for /etc/passwd is `644` (`rw-r--r--`): root can write, everyone can read. That world-readability is essential because a huge number of library calls (`getpwuid`, `id`, `ls -l`, name resolution in shells) depend on ordinary users being able to look UIDs up to usernames. `chmod 640` breaks those lookups for anyone not in the file's group. `chmod 600` locks out non-root readers entirely and produces the same failures more severely. `chmod 444` also removes write permission from root, so `passwd`, `useradd`, `usermod` and `chsh` — which run as root — cannot rewrite the file.

questions.question: The administrator wants to give user `bob` read/write access to `/srv/project` via a POSIX ACL, WITHOUT changing the file's owner, group or classical mode bits. Which command does that?
options: `getfacl -m u:bob:rw /srv/project` — `getfacl` only DISPLAYS ACLs; `-m` is not one of its flags
`chown bob /srv/project && chmod 664 /srv/project` — changes the owner and the classic mode bits, violating the requirement
`setfacl -m u:bob:rw /srv/project` — `-m` MODIFIES ACLs, adding the u:bob:rw entry without touching UGO bits
`setfacl -x u:bob /srv/project` — `-x` REMOVES an ACL entry, not adds one
questions.explanation: `setfacl -m u:bob:rw /srv/project` modifies the extended ACL to add an entry granting user `bob` read/write while leaving owner, group and the classical mode bits alone. `getfacl` is strictly a reader; it prints ACLs and has no `-m` option. `setfacl -x u:bob` removes any ACL entry for bob rather than adding one. `chown bob && chmod 664` DOES give bob write access, but by changing the owner and the mode bits it violates the requirement to leave them untouched.

questions.question: Members of the group `developers` should be able to run `systemctl restart httpd` as root through sudo, with NO password prompt, and nothing else. Which /etc/sudoers entry is correct?
options: `developers ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: ALL` — no leading `%` means this rule applies to a USER called `developers`, not the group; also grants ALL commands
`%developers ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart httpd` — `%` marks the group, target user is root (implied by ALL), NOPASSWD skips the prompt, command is fully qualified
`%developers ALL=(root) /bin/systemctl restart httpd` — targets the group and the right command, BUT no NOPASSWD so sudo still prompts
`developers ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart httpd` — missing the `%`, so this applies to a user literally named `developers`
questions.explanation: In sudoers, `%developers` targets the GROUP `developers` (without `%` it means a user of that name). `ALL=(ALL)` lets any member run the rule on any host as any user (including root), `NOPASSWD:` skips the password prompt, and the fully-qualified path `/bin/systemctl restart httpd` restricts them to exactly that one command. Option A grants `ALL` commands and applies to a user, not a group. Option C targets the group and the right command but omits NOPASSWD, so sudo still prompts. Option D uses the right command and NOPASSWD but drops the `%`, so the rule matches a user named `developers`, not the group.

questions.question: A production sshd should reject password logins entirely (keys only) AND forbid direct root SSH access. Which pair of `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` settings enforces BOTH?
options: `PasswordAuthentication no` + `PermitRootLogin no` — passwords disabled, root SSH disabled outright
`PasswordAuthentication no` + `PermitRootLogin without-password` — passwords disabled, but root can still log in via key
`PubkeyAuthentication no` + `PermitRootLogin no` — DISABLES key auth, leaving only passwords (weakens the box)
`PasswordAuthentication no` + `PermitRootLogin yes` — passwords disabled but root SSH remains open
questions.explanation: `PasswordAuthentication no` refuses password-based logins so only keys (or other configured methods) work; `PermitRootLogin no` blocks any SSH login as root, key OR password. `PermitRootLogin without-password` (also spelt `prohibit-password` on OpenSSH ≥7.0) permits root via keys — that violates "forbid direct root SSH". Setting `PubkeyAuthentication no` turns off keys and leaves the server relying on passwords, which is the opposite of the goal. `PermitRootLogin yes` keeps root SSH wide open.

questions.question: On a legacy box running `iptables`, the administrator wants to drop all incoming TCP traffic destined for port 23 (Telnet), from any source. Which command adds the correct rule?
options: `iptables -I OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 23 -j REJECT` — filters OUTBOUND traffic and only affects packets THIS host originates
`iptables -A FORWARD -p tcp --dport 23 -j DROP` — FORWARD applies to routed traffic passing THROUGH, not destined for this host
`iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --sport 23 -j DROP` — matches packets whose SOURCE port is 23 (return traffic), not connections TO port 23
`iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 23 -j DROP` — appends to INPUT, matches TCP with destination port 23, silently drops
questions.explanation: The INPUT chain is what handles traffic destined for the local host; `-p tcp --dport 23` matches TCP packets whose DESTINATION port is 23; `-j DROP` silently discards them. `-A` appends the rule to the end of the chain — swap for `-I` if you want it inserted at the top. The other options fail on scope: `OUTPUT` filters what THIS host sends, `FORWARD` filters traffic being routed through this host to somewhere else, and `--sport 23` matches packets FROM port 23 (return traffic from a Telnet client if you were the server, not new incoming Telnet sessions).

questions.question: SELinux is enforcing. A web application cannot WRITE to `/var/app/uploads` even though the directory is chmod 777. Which is the most likely cause AND the correct fix?
options: The SELinux type label on the directory is wrong (e.g. `default_t`); run `chcon -Rt httpd_sys_rw_content_t /var/app/uploads` and use `semanage fcontext` for persistence
The `httpd_can_network_connect` boolean is off — but that boolean controls OUTBOUND network access, not filesystem writes
The httpd process runs as the wrong Unix user; add it to the `apache` group with `usermod -aG apache www-data` — Unix perms are already 777, so this cannot be the cause
The directory needs the sticky bit (`chmod 1777`) — sticky affects DELETION rules on shared dirs, not writes
questions.explanation: When SELinux is enforcing, the Unix mode bits are necessary but not sufficient — MAC also checks the type label. httpd runs confined as `httpd_t` and is only allowed to WRITE to files typed `httpd_sys_rw_content_t` (and a few others). A path that inherited `default_t` or `var_t` when it was created will refuse writes despite mode 777. Immediate fix: `chcon -Rt httpd_sys_rw_content_t /var/app/uploads`; for a persistent one that survives `restorecon`, add `semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_rw_content_t "/var/app/uploads(/.*)?"`. The `httpd_can_network_connect` boolean is about outbound TCP, not the filesystem. Adding httpd to the apache group is orthogonal — 777 already gave everyone write. Sticky bit only limits WHO CAN DELETE files, not who can write them.

questions.question: The administrator sees repeated sudo failures in `/var/log/auth.log` for user `mallory`. Which command filters the systemd journal to entries emitted by the `sudo` binary that mention `mallory`?
options: `journalctl -u sudo --since today | grep mallory` — `sudo` is not a systemd UNIT, so `-u sudo` matches nothing on most systems
`journalctl -xe --identifier=sudo` — filters by syslog identifier `sudo` but shows ALL sudo entries, not just mallory's
`journalctl _COMM=sudo | grep -i mallory` — matches journal records where the emitting command was `sudo` (COMM field), then greps for mallory
`journalctl -f /var/log/auth.log` — `journalctl` reads the binary journal, not text files; passing a log-file path is a syntax error
questions.explanation: systemd-journald stores structured fields, one of which (`_COMM`) is the command name of the process that logged the entry. `journalctl _COMM=sudo` returns every record emitted by a sudo invocation; piping to `grep -i mallory` narrows it to entries mentioning her username. `journalctl -u sudo` matches by systemd UNIT, and sudo is not one, so it yields nothing. `--identifier=sudo` matches the SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER field (very close to `_COMM=sudo` here) but on its own returns every sudo record, not just mallory's — piping to grep would fix that, and this option omits the pipe. `journalctl -f /var/log/auth.log` mixes flags: `journalctl` reads the binary journal (not text log files) and does not accept a file path as a positional argument.

questions.question: A developer has imported a colleague's public GPG key (uid `colleague@example.com`) into the local keyring. Which command encrypts `report.txt` so ONLY the colleague can decrypt it?
options: `gpg --gen-key colleague@example.com report.txt` — `--gen-key` starts an INTERACTIVE key-pair creation wizard; it does not encrypt files
`gpg --sign -r colleague@example.com report.txt` — signs the file to prove authorship; produces a cleartext-plus-signature, not ciphertext
`gpg --encrypt -r colleague@example.com report.txt` — encrypts to the colleague's public key; only their matching private key can decrypt
`gpg --decrypt -r colleague@example.com report.txt` — DECRYPTS existing ciphertext; useless when you have plaintext
questions.explanation: `gpg --encrypt -r <uid> <file>` encrypts the file to the recipient identified by the UID (`-r` for --recipient), producing `report.txt.gpg` that only the holder of the matching private key can open. `--sign` produces a signed but READABLE artefact (integrity, not confidentiality). `--decrypt` runs the reverse operation — it needs ciphertext as input, not plaintext. `--gen-key` is the interactive key-pair generation wizard and does not accept a filename to encrypt.

questions.question: AppArmor is installed and there is a profile for `/usr/sbin/nginx`. The administrator wants to switch that profile into COMPLAIN mode (log denials, do not block) for testing. Which command does it?
options: `aa-complain /usr/sbin/nginx` — flips the named profile into complain (learning) mode; denials get logged, not blocked
`setenforce 0` — the SELinux command for permissive mode; AppArmor ignores it entirely
`aa-enforce /usr/sbin/nginx` — moves the profile into ENFORCE mode, the OPPOSITE of what is asked
`apparmor_parser -R /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.nginx` — REMOVES (unloads) the profile from the kernel, no complain mode
questions.explanation: `aa-complain <path-or-profile>` toggles the profile into complain mode: the kernel still evaluates the policy but logs denials to `dmesg`/audit instead of blocking, which is perfect for testing new rules. `setenforce 0` is an SELinux tool and has zero effect on AppArmor. `aa-enforce` is the opposite command — it moves a profile back into ENFORCE. `apparmor_parser -R` (remove) unloads the profile from the kernel entirely, so nginx runs unconfined and no learning happens.

questions.question: A Bash loop `for f in *.log; do gzip $f; done` fails on filenames that contain spaces. Which fix quotes the variable so gzip sees each filename as a single argument?
options: `for f in *.log; do gzip ${f}; done` — brace form; still unquoted, so word-splitting on spaces remains
`for f in "*.log"; do gzip $f; done` — quotes prevent GLOB expansion; the literal string `*.log` becomes the only iterated value
`for f in *.log; do gzip '$f'; done` — single quotes pass the literal characters `$f` to gzip, not the variable value
`for f in *.log; do gzip "$f"; done` — double-quoted expansion keeps each filename (spaces included) as one shell word
questions.explanation: Only `"$f"` (double-quoted parameter expansion) protects filenames with spaces from being split into multiple arguments. `${f}` clarifies where the variable name ends but still expands unquoted, so word-splitting kicks in. `"*.log"` prevents glob expansion — the loop iterates the LITERAL string `*.log` once, not the matching files. `'$f'` passes the literal three-character string `$f` to gzip; single quotes suppress variable expansion entirely.

questions.question: A Bash script exits with status code 127. What does exit code 127 specifically mean in Bash?
options: `Command not found` — Bash could not locate the requested executable in PATH (typo or missing binary)
`Permission denied` — Bash found the executable but the user lacks execute permission (exit 126 is the actual code for that)
`Segmentation fault` — a SIGSEGV kill produces status 139 (128+11), not 127
Successful exit — status 0 signals success; non-zero always signals an error
questions.explanation: In Bash, 127 is the well-defined status for `command not found` — typo in the command name, missing binary, or wrong PATH. `Permission denied on an executable file` is 126 (found but not executable). A segfault is reported as 128 + signal number = 139 for SIGSEGV, not 127. Exit code 0 means success by convention; anything non-zero means an error, but the specific code 127 always means "not found".

questions.question: The administrator wants to list every username on the system by extracting the FIRST colon-delimited field from `/etc/passwd`. Which command prints just the usernames, one per line?
options: `sed -n '3p' /etc/passwd` — prints the THIRD LINE of the file, unrelated to per-line field extraction
`cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd` — sets the delimiter to `:` and extracts field 1 (the username)
`cut -d: -f3 /etc/passwd` — extracts field 3, which is the numeric UID, not the username
`awk -F, '{print $1}' /etc/passwd` — sets the field separator to a COMMA, so /etc/passwd's colon layout is not split correctly
questions.explanation: The username is field 1 of /etc/passwd (`user:x:UID:GID:GECOS:home:shell`). `cut -d: -f1` sets the delimiter to `:` and prints the first field for every line, giving the username list. `cut -d: -f3` would emit UIDs instead. `sed -n '3p'` prints the third LINE of the file — the third user's whole entry, not usernames. `awk -F,` splits on comma, so /etc/passwd (which has no commas in most fields) prints each whole line, not the username. The correct awk equivalent would be `awk -F: '{print $1}'`.

questions.question: A Bash script must check that `/var/log/app.log` exists AND is a regular file (not a directory, symlink target that vanished, socket, or block device) before it reads from it. Which conditional test fits?
options: `[ -x /var/log/app.log ]` — tests EXECUTABILITY, unrelated to file-type filtering
`[ -e /var/log/app.log ]` — tests EXISTENCE but does not distinguish regular files from directories/sockets/devices
`[ -d /var/log/app.log ]` — tests for a DIRECTORY, which is the opposite of what we want
`[ -f /var/log/app.log ]` — tests that the path exists AND that stat() reports it as a regular file
questions.explanation: `[ -f PATH ]` is the classical regular-file predicate: it returns true if the path both exists AND `stat()` reports it as a regular file (mode `S_IFREG`). `[ -e PATH ]` is the pure existence check and does not filter by type — directories, sockets, char/block devices and FIFOs all pass. `[ -d PATH ]` is the directory predicate — the opposite of what the scenario needs. `[ -x PATH ]` checks the effective UID has execute permission; it has nothing to do with file type filtering. (For symlinks, `-f` follows the link and returns true only if the target is a regular file, which is usually what a log-reading script wants.)

questions.question: A script needs to print how many LINES in `/var/log/app.log` contain the word `ERROR`, and nothing else. Which is the MOST concise correct command?
options: `grep ERROR /var/log/app.log | wc -l` — correct count of matching lines, but requires an extra pipe and a second process
`grep -c ERROR /var/log/app.log` — `-c` makes grep emit just the count of matching lines, single process, exact requirement
`awk '/ERROR/ {count++} END {print count}' /var/log/app.log` — works, but more verbose than grep -c
`grep ERROR /var/log/app.log | tail -1` — prints the LAST matching line, not a count at all
questions.explanation: `grep -c PATTERN FILE` prints just the number of matching LINES, using a single grep process — this is the concise correct answer. `grep ... | wc -l` produces the same number but forks an extra `wc` and adds a pipe. The awk one-liner works but is bulkier; also, if a line contains `ERROR` twice, both grep-based counts (and this awk pattern) still count that line only once — they all agree, but grep -c is the simplest. `grep ERROR ... | tail -1` returns the last matching LINE, not a count.

questions.question: The administrator wants to replace EVERY occurrence of `localhost` with `127.0.0.1` in `/etc/myapp.conf`, editing the file in place. Which sed command does it?
options: `sed -i 's/localhost/127.0.0.1/g' /etc/myapp.conf` — `-i` edits in place; `s///g` substitutes every occurrence on each line
`sed -i 's/localhost/127.0.0.1/' /etc/myapp.conf` — edits in place BUT without `g`, only the FIRST match on each line is replaced
`sed '/localhost/127.0.0.1/g' /etc/myapp.conf` — syntax error: missing the leading `s` for the substitution command
`sed 's/localhost/127.0.0.1/' /etc/myapp.conf` — prints to stdout only (no -i) and misses subsequent occurrences on a line (no g)
questions.explanation: The correct incantation is `sed -i 's/localhost/127.0.0.1/g' /etc/myapp.conf`: `-i` rewrites the file in place, the `s///` command substitutes, and the `g` flag applies the substitution to EVERY match on each line, not just the first. Without `g` you get one replacement per line (option B). Without `-i` you get output on stdout and no file modification (option D). Option C is invalid sed syntax — the substitution command begins with the letter `s`.

questions.question: A developer has just run `git add .` on a fresh repo and wants to preview the exact diff that the NEXT `git commit` will record. Which command prints that diff?
options: `git log --stat` — shows historical commits and per-file line counts; the repo has no commits yet, so nothing is printed
`git diff --cached` — diffs the INDEX (staging area) against HEAD, showing exactly what will be committed
`git status --short` — lists file states in the porcelain format but does not print any actual line diff
`git diff` — diffs the WORKING TREE against the INDEX; after `git add .` there are no unstaged changes so this is empty
questions.explanation: `git diff --cached` (alias `git diff --staged`) compares the INDEX to HEAD, so it prints exactly the diff that a `git commit` would record. `git diff` with no flags compares the WORKING TREE to the INDEX; after `git add .` there are no unstaged deltas left, so it shows nothing. `git status --short` reports each file's state (A, M, ??) but does not emit a hunk-by-hunk diff. `git log --stat` walks commit history — on a repo that has never been committed to (or one where you want to see uncommitted changes), it does not answer the question at all.

questions.question: A developer wants to create a NEW branch `feature/auth` from the current HEAD and switch to it in a SINGLE command. Which git command does that?
options: `git clone --branch feature/auth` — `git clone` copies a remote repo; needs a URL and does not create a local feature branch
`git switch feature/auth` — switches to an EXISTING branch; use `git switch -c feature/auth` for creating one
`git branch feature/auth && git checkout feature/auth` — technically works, but that is TWO commands, not one
`git checkout -b feature/auth` — the classic one-shot form: creates the branch AND switches to it
questions.explanation: `git checkout -b feature/auth` combines branch creation with checkout in a single command, which is exactly the requirement. `git branch feature/auth && git checkout feature/auth` gets the same result, but as two chained commands, not one. `git switch feature/auth` (introduced in Git 2.23 as a cleaner split of checkout) requires the branch to already exist; the equivalent one-shot form is `git switch -c feature/auth`. `git clone` fetches a remote repository and does not create a local topic branch from the current HEAD.

questions.question: A Dockerfile copies requirements.txt AND runs `pip install` BEFORE copying the application source. Why is that ordering deliberate?
options: Layer caching — each Dockerfile step is cached by its inputs, so pip install runs only when requirements.txt actually changes; app-code edits skip that layer and rebuild in seconds
`COPY` semantics — the instruction refuses to execute if application source is placed on the working layer before requirements.txt, so the ordering is a hard build-graph requirement
`pip` parsing — the interpreter cannot process app code at build time until requirements.txt has been placed at the image root as a manifest for the dependency solver
`FROM` constraints — a base image resolves runtime dependencies at pull time and refuses application files that arrive before the dependency manifest has been declared
questions.explanation: The Docker build cache is the reason. Each instruction is hashed against its inputs; if the requirements.txt file is unchanged, Docker reuses the cached layer for the pip-install step, and only re-runs the `COPY .` and later layers when app code changes. Put `COPY . /app` first and the requirements install becomes part of a layer that changes on every code edit, invalidating the cache every time. `COPY` does not care what has been copied before it. `pip` does not need any specific ordering to "parse" app code (it does not, in fact). `FROM` sets the base image; it has no rule about dependency ordering.

questions.question: In `docker run -d -v /host/data:/container/data:ro nginx`, what does the `:ro` suffix on the volume mount do?
options: The bind mount `/host/data → /container/data` is mounted READ-ONLY inside the container
The ENTIRE container filesystem is made immutable, equivalent to `docker run --read-only`
The `nginx` image itself is pulled from a read-only image registry
The container process runs with restricted (Read-Only) capabilities, similar to dropping CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE
questions.explanation: In Docker volume syntax `HOST:CONTAINER[:mode]`, `:ro` marks this SPECIFIC mount as read-only inside the container. The container can `read()` from `/container/data` but every `write()` returns EROFS. Other mounts and the container's own writable overlay layer are unaffected. Making the entire container root filesystem immutable is a separate switch, `docker run --read-only`. `:ro` has nothing to do with registry access or the process's capabilities/security profile.

questions.question: A cron job must run `/opt/backup.sh` every day at 2:30 AM. Which crontab entry is correct? (Cron field order: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week.)
options: `0 2 30 * * /opt/backup.sh` — runs at 02:00 on the 30th of each month; that is minute 0, hour 2, day-of-month 30, so it fires monthly, not daily
`2 30 * * * /opt/backup.sh` — puts 30 in the HOUR field; hour 30 is out of range (0–23) and most cron implementations reject or silently skip the line
`30 2 * * * /opt/backup.sh` — minute 30, hour 2, every day of month, every month, every day of week — evaluates to 02:30 daily, exactly what the task asks
`* * 2 30 * /opt/backup.sh` — every minute of every hour on day-of-month 2, in month 30; month 30 does not exist so this line never fires at all
questions.explanation: The cron field order is minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week. `30 2 * * *` is minute 30 of hour 2, every day, every month, every weekday — exactly 02:30 daily. `0 2 30 * *` fires at 02:00, but only on the 30th of every month. `2 30 * * *` puts 30 in the HOUR field, which is out of the 0–23 range and either rejected or clamped depending on cron implementation. `* * 2 30 *` is well-formed but nonsensical: every minute of every hour on day-of-month 2, in month 30 (invalid) — so it never runs at all.

questions.question: An Ansible task must install the `nginx` package on Debian-family hosts AND ensure the LATEST available version is present. Which task definition is correct?
options:
```yaml
- name: Install nginx (yum)
  yum:
    name: nginx
    state: latest
```
`yum:` targets RHEL-family hosts, not Debian

```yaml
- name: Install nginx (package)
  package:
    name: nginx
    state: present
```
`state: present` only ensures the package exists, not that it is the newest version

```yaml
- name: Install nginx (apt)
  apt:
    name: nginx
    state: latest
    update_cache: yes
```
`apt:` is the Debian-family module, `state: latest` upgrades to the newest, `update_cache: yes` refreshes the index first

```yaml
- name: Install nginx (apt)
  apt:
    name: nginx
    state: present
```
Debian-family module, but `state: present` only guarantees existence, not latest
questions.explanation: The `apt` module is Ansible's Debian-family package manager; `state: latest` upgrades the package to the newest version available in the enabled repos, and `update_cache: yes` runs the equivalent of `apt-get update` first so the metadata is fresh. `yum:` is the RHEL-family module and will not run on Debian hosts. `package:` is a generic wrapper that dispatches to the right underlying module; combined with `state: present` it only ensures the package is installed, not upgraded. `apt` with `state: present` has the same problem — it does not upgrade an already-installed nginx.

questions.question: A Bash function `check_connectivity` returns 0 on success or 1 on failure. What is the correct way to CAPTURE that return code into a shell variable?
options: `result=check_connectivity()` — Bash treats this as an ASSIGNMENT of the literal string `check_connectivity()`, the function is not run
`check_connectivity; result=$?` — runs the function and then reads `$?`, which holds the exit status of the last command
`result=$(check_connectivity)` — captures STDOUT, not the exit code; `result` ends up with any text the function printed
`export result; check_connectivity` — declares `result` as an environment variable before the function runs; nothing writes to it
questions.explanation: `$?` is Bash's built-in variable holding the exit status of the last foreground command or function, so `check_connectivity; result=$?` runs the function and captures its return code. `result=check_connectivity()` is not a call at all — Bash sees a variable assignment of a literal string with `()` glued on and never invokes the function. `result=$(check_connectivity)` runs the function in a subshell and captures its STDOUT, so `result` holds any echoed text rather than the exit code. `export result; check_connectivity` merely marks `result` for export; nothing writes to it.

questions.question: `top` shows a load average of `18.5 14.2 9.8` on a 4-core system. What does this indicate?
options: The three numbers report memory usage in gigabytes over 1, 5 and 15 minutes — but load average has always been process-queue depth, not memory, so this reading has nothing to do with RAM
There was a brief 15-minute spike that has almost fully recovered and the system is now essentially healthy — but 18.5 at 1 min on 4 cores is far too high to call recovered
The system is severely overloaded — 4.6× more runnable/uninterruptible processes than the machine has cores; the trend IS decreasing but is still well above healthy on a 4-core box
The system is healthy — load averages above 10 are normal on any modern multi-core box, but that is a myth: healthy load is relative to core count, not an absolute number
questions.explanation: Linux load average counts the average number of processes in R (running) or D (uninterruptible sleep) state over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. On a 4-core box, a load equal to 4 means fully saturated; anything higher means processes are queuing. 18.5 on the 1-min figure is 4.6× cores — badly overloaded. The 5-min (14.2) and 15-min (9.8) numbers ARE lower, so the trend is downward, but they are still well above 4, so the box is far from healthy. Load averages are process-queue depth, not memory. There is no fixed "load above 10 = normal" rule — normal depends on core count.

questions.question: The administrator wants to capture all TCP traffic on interface `eth0` with destination or source port 443 to a pcap file for later analysis in Wireshark. Which tcpdump invocation is correct?
options: `tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/capture.pcap tcp port 443` — captures on eth0, filter `tcp port 443`, writes raw packets to a pcap file
`tcpdump -i eth0 port 443` — captures on eth0 and port 443, but only prints to stdout; no pcap is written
`tcpdump --interface eth0 --port 443 --write /tmp/capture.pcap` — tcpdump does not accept these long-option names
`tcpdump -i eth0 tcp:443 > /tmp/capture.pcap` — `tcp:443` is not valid BPF syntax, and `> file` captures TEXT output, not a pcap
questions.explanation: `tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/capture.pcap tcp port 443` sets the interface (`-i`), writes raw packets to a pcap file (`-w`), and uses BPF filter `tcp port 443` to match TCP traffic where the source OR destination port is 443. The `-w` flag is essential — without it (option B) tcpdump only prints a decoded summary to stdout. Redirecting stdout with `> file` (option D) captures the text summary, not a binary pcap Wireshark can read; also `tcp:443` is not valid BPF syntax (the correct form is `tcp port 443`). tcpdump does not accept the `--interface`, `--port`, `--write` long options shown in option C.

questions.question: After a kernel update, the box refuses to boot with `Kernel panic - not syncing: VFS: Unable to mount root fs`. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The GRUB config is pointing at the wrong kernel version — but a wrong entry usually boots the OTHER kernel instead of panicking here
The root filesystem has a journal error — but journal errors surface AFTER the root is mounted, with different messages
The new kernel's initramfs is missing or does not contain the storage/HBA driver the root device needs (SCSI, NVMe, RAID, encryption)
The /etc/fstab entry for the root has an incorrect UUID — but fstab is not consulted until AFTER the kernel mounts the initial root
questions.explanation: The panic `VFS: Unable to mount root fs` fires when the kernel has finished loading initramfs and cannot find or open a working root block device. That almost always means the initramfs is missing a driver the kernel needs to see the disk — a SCSI/AHCI/NVMe HBA module, a software RAID or dm-crypt setup, or a filesystem module. A wrong GRUB default typically boots the OTHER kernel; even when it names a bad initramfs the error path is different. Filesystem journal errors happen AFTER the root is mounted (options B/D). fstab is not read until the initramfs pivot-root completes — VFS mount fails before that.

questions.question: A cloned RHEL VM boots with SELinux in enforcing mode and MANY files have wrong labels because the clone bypassed the source's relabel. The administrator wants to trigger a full filesystem relabel on the NEXT reboot. Which is the standard trigger?
options: `touch /.autorelabel` — creates the flag file the init scripts look for; on reboot the system relabels and reboots itself again
`fixfiles -F onboot` — schedules a similar boot-time relabel; less commonly documented and specific to policycoreutils
`semanage fcontext -a -t root_t '/'` — adds a POLICY rule, does not trigger a relabel run
`restorecon -Rv /` — relabels IMMEDIATELY on the live filesystem, may miss busy files and is not the standard next-boot mechanism
questions.explanation: `touch /.autorelabel` is the canonical trigger: the RHEL init scripts detect the flag on early boot, do a full `restorecon` across the filesystem, remove the flag and reboot the machine once more. It works even on files that would be busy on a running system. `fixfiles -F onboot` is a valid alternative and shares the same mechanism, but `/.autorelabel` is what the exam and Red Hat docs recommend first. `semanage fcontext -a -t root_t '/'` writes a POLICY entry — no relabel actually runs from that command alone. `restorecon -Rv /` relabels immediately but on a live system it can miss files that are locked or bind-mounted, and does not benefit from the early-boot single-user context autorelabel uses.

questions.question: A user reports "disk full" errors, but `df -h` shows the filesystem at only 60% usage. Which is the MOST likely cause?
options: LVM thin provisioning is reporting POOL capacity rather than volume capacity — shows up in vgs/lvs, not on df
The filesystem was mounted `noatime`, which skews usage reporting — noatime affects atime updates, not `df` accounting
Inodes are exhausted — `df -h` shows block usage but the filesystem has run out of inodes so no new files can be created (check with `df -i`)
Large files have been deleted but processes still hold them open — that scenario keeps SPACE reserved, so `df -h` would show HIGH, not 60%, usage
questions.explanation: `df -h` reports BLOCK usage; a filesystem can be block-fine but out of INODES, at which point `open(..., O_CREAT)` fails with ENOSPC. `df -i` shows inode usage; on inode-exhausted volumes it reads 100% while `df -h` still reads 60%. Deleted-but-open files (option D) actually SHOW as used space on df — they cannot be reclaimed until the process closes the fd — so `df -h` would report high, not 60%. LVM thin-pool exhaustion is real but shows up in `vgs`/`lvs`/`dmsetup` and produces I/O errors, not a `disk full` from userspace at the filesystem layer. `noatime` disables access-time updates for performance and has no effect on df accounting.

questions.question: `ip route show` prints `default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0`. External connections time out, but `ping 192.168.1.1` succeeds. What should the administrator investigate NEXT?
options: Run `systemctl restart networking` — routes are correct and reachable; restarting the service will not change anything upstream
MTU on eth0 may be wrong — run `ip link set eth0 mtu 1500`; MTU mismatches cause size-dependent drops, not universal timeouts one hop out
Add a static route `ip route add 0.0.0.0/0 via 192.168.1.1` — the default route already exists, so adding a duplicate has no effect
Investigate whether the gateway 192.168.1.1 has its OWN internet reachability (or if firewall/NAT on it is blocking outbound sessions)
questions.explanation: The routing table is correct AND the gateway itself is up (ping to `192.168.1.1` succeeds), so the fault sits UPSTREAM of the gateway. Typical causes: the router has lost its own uplink, its NAT/firewall rules are blocking or SNATing incorrectly, or the ISP session is down. Adding a duplicate default route (option C) does nothing because one already exists. Restarting `networking` does not change upstream reachability. An MTU issue would show as size-sensitive symptoms (small packets fine, large ones dropped mid-session), not a full timeout to every external destination.

questions.question: `/var` is 100% full because of accumulated rotated logs in `/var/log`. Which action BOTH reclaims space now AND prevents recurrence?
options: `truncate -s 0 /var/log/syslog && systemctl restart rsyslog` — reclaims space from a single file and restarts the logger, but does nothing to stop the same files from ballooning again
`rm -rf /var/log/* && echo 'maxsize 100M' >> /etc/logrotate.conf` — reclaims space aggressively but deletes ACTIVE log files, breaks live loggers and destroys the directory layout services expect
`find /var/log -name '*.gz' -mtime +30 -delete` and add a per-service logrotate policy (size/maxage/rotate count) — reclaims space by removing old archives AND caps future growth
`mount --bind /tmp /var/log` — hides existing logs behind a tmpfs mount, never actually reclaims space on /var, and puts new logs on a volatile filesystem that clears at reboot
questions.explanation: The safe reclamation pattern is to remove OLD compressed archives (`find /var/log -name '*.gz' -mtime +30 -delete`) — never live log files — and then tighten logrotate (`maxsize`, `rotate N`, `maxage`) so the archives cannot balloon again. `rm -rf /var/log/*` blows away directory layout and active files that services have open, which typically breaks logging until services are restarted and directories re-created. `truncate` only shrinks one file and leaves the rotation policy unchanged. Bind-mounting `/tmp` onto `/var/log` hides the old logs (they still occupy /var), sends new logs to a volatile mount and does not reclaim any space.

questions.question: A systemd service `webapp` shows `Active: failed (Result: exit-code)`. Which command shows the process's own stdout/stderr as captured by systemd so the administrator can see WHY it exited?
options: `cat /var/log/webapp.log` — assumes the service writes to that file; many modern services log to stdout, which is captured by the journal instead
`dmesg | grep webapp` — dmesg is the kernel ring buffer; it does not contain userspace stdout/stderr
`systemctl show webapp` — prints the unit's PROPERTIES (ExecStart, Restart, etc.) in key=value form; no runtime logs
`journalctl -u webapp -n 100 --no-pager` — pulls the last 100 journal entries for the webapp UNIT, including stdout/stderr that systemd captured
questions.explanation: systemd captures every unit's stdout and stderr into the journal, tagged with the unit name. `journalctl -u webapp -n 100` (or `-e` to jump to the end) is the exact query for a failed unit's own runtime output, including the last few lines that immediately preceded the failure. `systemctl show webapp` prints property key=value pairs (ExecStart, Restart, MainPID) — no log data. `dmesg` is the kernel ring buffer; userspace stdout does not go there. Assuming `/var/log/webapp.log` exists is only correct if the daemon opens that file itself — many packaged services now rely on journald.

questions.question: Alice cannot log in with her password. /etc/shadow shows her entry as `alice:!$6$hash...:19000:0:90:7:::`. What does the `!` prefix on the second field mean?
options: The account requires 2FA — /etc/shadow does not encode 2FA state, that is configured in PAM
The account is LOCKED — the `!` makes the stored hash impossible to match, so no supplied password can log in (this is what `usermod -L` does)
The field uses a hashing algorithm other than SHA-512 — the algorithm is signalled by the `$id$` prefix (`$6$` here means SHA-512) regardless of `!`
The account has never had a password set — an unset password shows as an empty field or `*`, not `!hash`
questions.explanation: A `!` (or `!!`) prefix on the /etc/shadow password field marks the account as LOCKED: the crypt algorithm can never produce a hash that starts with `!`, so no password supplied via PAM will match. That is exactly the state `usermod -L` and `passwd -l` leave the field in. 2FA is configured in PAM stacks, not by /etc/shadow markers. The hashing algorithm is indicated by the `$id$` prefix (`$6$` = SHA-512, `$5$` = SHA-256, `$y$` = yescrypt) and is independent of the leading `!`. An empty password would show as an empty field or `*`, not `!hash`.

questions.question: The administrator wants to see every LISTENING TCP socket on the local host along with the OWNING process (PID and program name), in a compact one-line-per-socket format. Which command does it?
options: `netstat -a` — shows every socket (listening and established) but not just listeners, and without `-p` it does not include PID/program
`ss -tlnp` — TCP (`-t`), listening only (`-l`), numeric (`-n`), with process info (`-p`) — exactly what is asked
`lsof -i :8080` — shows fd usage for ONE specific port; excellent tool, but not the compact all-listeners view
`ip link show` — reports network INTERFACE link state (up/down, MAC, MTU); says nothing about sockets
questions.explanation: `ss -tlnp` — from the modern iproute2 suite — is the direct answer: `-t` restricts to TCP, `-l` to listening sockets, `-n` prevents port-name resolution, `-p` adds the PID and program name. `netstat -a` returns EVERY socket state (including ESTABLISHED and TIME_WAIT), and without `-p` and `-l` you do not get the requested compact listener-only view with process info; on many distros netstat is also deprecated in favour of ss. `lsof -i :8080` is great for a single-port drill-down, but the question asks for the full listener enumeration. `ip link show` reports interface link state (up/down, MTU, MAC), not socket state.

questions.question: `vmstat 1 5` shows the `wa` column consistently around 80%. What does that mean?
options: 80% of CPU time was consumed by USERSPACE processes — that is the `us` column, not `wa`
The network interface is saturated and packets are queuing — vmstat does not report network state on its main line
The CPUs are sitting IDLE waiting for I/O to return — I/O (usually disk) is the current bottleneck
Memory is being swapped hard — swap I/O appears in the `si`/`so` columns of vmstat, not `wa`
questions.explanation: `wa` in `vmstat` is iowait — the percentage of time the CPU was IDLE while there was at least one outstanding I/O request. High and sustained wa (say, above 20–30%) usually points to the disk subsystem as the bottleneck. User-space CPU time is the `us` column. Swap activity is reported in `si` (swap-in) and `so` (swap-out). Network saturation is not reported directly by vmstat — you would use `sar -n DEV`, `ip -s link` or `iftop` for that.

questions.question: After installing a new storage driver on a RHEL/CentOS system, the administrator needs to regenerate initramfs for the CURRENTLY RUNNING kernel so the new module is included at next boot. Which command is correct?
options: `update-initramfs -u` — Debian/Ubuntu's initramfs-tools wrapper; not shipped on RHEL/CentOS, which use the dracut generator instead
`grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg` — regenerates the GRUB boot-menu configuration only; does not rebuild initramfs images at all
`mkinitrd /boot/initrd-$(uname -r).img $(uname -r)` — the legacy Red Hat generator, superseded by dracut on all modern RHEL/CentOS releases
`dracut --force /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r).img $(uname -r)` — dracut is the RHEL initramfs generator; `--force` overwrites the existing image for that kernel
questions.explanation: On modern RHEL/CentOS (7+), `dracut` is the initramfs generator. `dracut --force <output> <kver>` regenerates the initramfs for the specified kernel version and `--force` allows overwriting an existing file. Interpolating `$(uname -r)` targets the currently running kernel. `update-initramfs -u` is the Debian/Ubuntu equivalent (uses initramfs-tools) and is not available on RHEL. `mkinitrd` is the older Red-Hat tool that was replaced by dracut. `grub2-mkconfig` regenerates GRUB configuration but does not rebuild the initramfs image.

questions.question: A Dockerfile ends with `CMD ["python", "app.py"]`. The container is started with `docker run myimage python debug.py`. Which command actually executes inside the container?
options: Both `app.py` and `debug.py` run in parallel — Docker treats CMD and run-args as merged commands
`python debug.py` — arguments supplied to `docker run` after the image name REPLACE the CMD entirely
An error is raised because the two commands conflict — Docker never raises this error; the run-args simply win
`python app.py` — CMD is baked into the image and cannot be overridden at run time
questions.explanation: When you pass arguments after the image name to `docker run`, they REPLACE the image's CMD. So `docker run myimage python debug.py` runs `python debug.py` and CMD is ignored for this container. ENTRYPOINT behaves differently — arguments become PARAMETERS appended to ENTRYPOINT — but the Dockerfile shown uses only CMD. There is no error path; overriding CMD at run time is a supported feature, not a conflict.

questions.question: The administrator wants to view ALL DNS record types for `example.com` (A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS, …) using standard troubleshooting tools. Which command is the standard choice?
options: `nslookup example.com` — legacy tool; defaults to A records only unless you set `type=ANY` in interactive mode
`host -a example.com` — valid alternative that queries multiple record types; less scriptable than dig
`ping -a example.com` — the `-a` flag on ping only means "audible bell on reply", it does not fetch other DNS record types
`dig example.com ANY` — dig with the `ANY` qtype requests every record the resolver will hand back for the name
questions.explanation: `dig example.com ANY` is the standard troubleshooting query for retrieving every record type in one call; it prints an authoritative-style answer section and is the tool most exam material recommends. `host -a` is a valid, more terse alternative and would also be accepted operationally. `nslookup` defaults to A records unless you use interactive `set type=ANY`, so a bare `nslookup example.com` does not meet the requirement. `ping -a` is a red herring — the `-a` flag has nothing to do with DNS record types (in some pings it emits an audible bell on reply, in others it maps to IP-address resolution). (Note: since 2019 many authoritative servers return HINFO/refuse for ANY per RFC 8482, so `dig` may not always return every record in practice — but as a documented exam answer for the standard tool, `dig ANY` is the choice.)

questions.question: A production system's GRUB2 menu has two kernel entries. The administrator edits `/etc/default/grub` and sets `GRUB_DEFAULT=0` so the newer kernel becomes the default. What must be run for the change to take effect?
options: `grub2-install /dev/sda` — reinstalls the bootloader to the MBR; does not rebuild grub.cfg from /etc/default/grub
`systemctl reboot` — reboots the machine but reads the OLD grub.cfg because it was never regenerated
`grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg` — rebuilds grub.cfg from /etc/default/grub and /etc/grub.d/*, applying the new setting
`update-grub && reboot` — `update-grub` is the Debian/Ubuntu wrapper name; on RHEL/CentOS it is `grub2-mkconfig`
questions.explanation: `grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg` (RHEL/CentOS) or `grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg` (some Debian derivatives) reads /etc/default/grub together with the scriptlets in /etc/grub.d/*, and writes a new grub.cfg. That is the step that translates `GRUB_DEFAULT=0` into a real change in the boot menu. `grub2-install` reinstalls the boot loader binary to the disk MBR/EFI partition — not the same as regenerating grub.cfg. `systemctl reboot` would just reboot with the stale grub.cfg. `update-grub` is Debian/Ubuntu's wrapper for grub-mkconfig — the intent is right but the tool is not available on RHEL/CentOS.

questions.question: The administrator needs a long-running Podman container `dataproc` that continues after the interactive login that started it ends. Which command starts the container so that it survives logout?
options: `podman run -d --name dataproc --restart always myimage` — `--restart always` on its own is not enough in rootless mode; you also need a generated systemd unit plus `loginctl enable-linger` to survive logout
`podman run --detach --name dataproc myimage` — `--detach` (`-d`) starts the container under the Podman/conmon supervisor detached from the launching shell, so it outlives the login session
`nohup podman run --name dataproc myimage &` — a shell-level trick to detach a foreground process from SIGHUP; works but is not the Podman-native way to run a long-lived container
`podman run --name dataproc myimage & disown` — same category as the nohup trick; runs in the background of the current shell then removes it from the shell's job table, not idiomatic Podman
questions.explanation: `podman run --detach --name dataproc myimage` starts the container detached under the Podman `conmon` supervisor; its lifecycle is independent of the shell that launched it, so logging out leaves it running. `--restart always` is not sufficient in rootless mode — it needs the container's systemd user unit (`podman generate systemd --new --files --name dataproc` + `systemctl --user enable ...` with `loginctl enable-linger`) to fire after logout. `nohup ... &` and `& disown` are shell techniques that also work in practice, but they are not the Podman-idiomatic pattern and can leave orphaned processes in some configurations.

questions.question: A bash script fails intermittently in production. To debug, the administrator wants to see every command EXECUTED with variables expanded and prefixed with `+`. Which invocation enables that trace mode?
options: `bash -e script.sh` — enables errexit so the script aborts on the FIRST command that returns non-zero; useful as a safety belt but prints no trace of what ran
`bash -v script.sh` — echoes each raw source line to stderr as it is READ from disk (before variable expansion), so you see the code but not the runtime values
`bash -x script.sh` — enables xtrace: every command is echoed to stderr prefixed with `+` after parameter expansion but before execution, so you see actual values
`bash -n script.sh` — enables noexec; the shell parses the script and reports any syntax error but never actually runs a command from it (dry-run parse)
questions.explanation: `bash -x` enables xtrace: each command is printed to stderr with a `+ ` prefix AFTER parameter and command substitution but BEFORE execution, so the actual expanded values are visible. `bash -v` prints the RAW source lines as they are read — helpful for parse errors but shows the unexpanded form. `bash -e` (errexit) aborts on the first failing command and prints nothing extra, so it is a safety mode, not a trace mode. `bash -n` (noexec) walks the syntax and reports parse errors without ever running the script.

questions.question: The administrator wants to enumerate the TCP ports the host is currently LISTENING on, with the owning process, from the command line. Which TWO commands display essentially the same listening-TCP-socket information on a modern Linux host?
options: `ss -tlnp` — iproute2 utility; lists TCP listeners with numeric ports and the owning process
`netstat -tlnp` — legacy net-tools utility; same output shape as `ss -tlnp` on systems that still ship it
`ip link show` — reports interface link state (up/down, MTU, MAC); says nothing about listening sockets
`lsof -i :22` — lists processes with fds on ONE specific port; targeted to a port, not the full listener set
questions.explanation: `ss -tlnp` (modern) and `netstat -tlnp` (legacy net-tools) both enumerate LISTENING (`-l`) TCP (`-t`) sockets in numeric form (`-n`) with the owning process (`-p`). Their output is functionally equivalent; ss is the current standard and netstat is being phased out on many distros but ships the same information where present. `lsof -i :22` is scoped to a single port (also useful, but different scope). `ip link show` is about interface link state, not sockets.
